```{r}
# Question 4: Kruskal-Wallis Test to Find the 9 Most Powerful Predictors
# Compute Kruskal-Wallis test statistics for each predictor
kruskal_stats <- sapply(prostate[, -1], function(x) kruskal.test(x ~ prostate$Y)$statistic)

# Sort predictors by test statistic in descending order
kruskal_sorted <- sort(kruskal_stats, decreasing = TRUE)

# Extract the top 9 predictors
top_9_predictors <- names(kruskal_sorted[1:9])
print("Top 9 Most Powerful Predictors:")
print(top_9_predictors)

```

```{r}
# Question 6: Create comparative boxplots
print(top_9_predictors)
# Ensure the required libraries are loaded
library(ggplot2)
library(reshape2)
library(stringdist)

# Print the top 9 predictors for verification
print(top_9_predictors)

# Match the top 9 predictors with column names in the dataset using string similarity
matched_predictors <- sapply(top_9_predictors, function(x) {
  colnames(prostate)[which.min(stringdist(x, colnames(prostate), method = "osa"))]
})

# Filter out only valid predictors (those that exist in the dataset)
valid_predictors <- matched_predictors[matched_predictors %in% colnames(prostate)]

if (length(valid_predictors) > 0) {
  # Ensure all selected predictors are numeric
  prostate[, valid_predictors] <- lapply(prostate[, valid_predictors], as.numeric)
  
  # Reshape the dataset to long format for ggplot2
  prostate_long <- melt(prostate, id.vars = "Y", measure.vars = valid_predictors)
  
  # Generate comparative boxplots with refined aesthetics
  ggplot(prostate_long, aes(x = as.factor(Y), y = value, fill = as.factor(Y))) +
    geom_boxplot(outlier.color = "black", outlier.shape = 16, alpha = 0.9) +
    geom_jitter(position = position_jitter(0.15), alpha = 0.4, size = 1.2, color = "gray30") +
    facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free_y", ncol = 3) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("#E69F00", "#56B4E9")) +  # Updated with soft contrasting colors
    theme_minimal() +
    labs(
      title = "Comparative Boxplots of Top Predictors",
      subtitle = "Distribution of Predictor Values by Response (Y: Cancer/Non-Cancer)",
      x = "Response Variable (Y)",
      y = "Predictor Value"
    ) +
    theme(
      strip.text = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold", color = "darkblue"),
      axis.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold"),
      axis.text = element_text(size = 10, color = "black"),
      legend.position = "none",
      plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12, hjust = 0.5, color = "gray40")
    )
} else {
  print("No valid predictors found for plotting.")
}
```

```{r}
# Question 8: Load necessary libraries
library(rpart)
library(rpart.plot)
library(ggplot2)
library(reshape2)

# Build the classification tree with cp = 0.01
tree_model <- rpart(Y ~ ., data = prostate, method = "class", control = rpart.control(cp = 0.01))

# Extract feature importance (weakest variables have the lowest importance)
importance <- tree_model$variable.importance

# Get the 9 weakest variables (lowest importance)
weakest_vars <- names(sort(importance, decreasing = FALSE))[1:9]

# Display the weakest variables
cat("9 weakest variables:\n")
cat(weakest_vars, sep = "\n")

# Ensure the selected predictors are numeric
prostate[, weakest_vars] <- lapply(prostate[, weakest_vars], as.numeric)

# Reshape the dataset to long format for ggplot2
prostate_long <- reshape2::melt(prostate, id.vars = "Y", measure.vars = weakest_vars)

# Generate comparative boxplots
ggplot(prostate_long, aes(x = as.factor(Y), y = value, fill = as.factor(Y))) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.color = "black", outlier.shape = 16, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_jitter(position = position_jitter(0.2), alpha = 0.5, size = 1, color = "gray40") +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free_y", ncol = 3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#FF9999", "#99CCFF")) +  # Custom colors
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Comparative Boxplots of 9 Weakest Variables",
       x = "Response Variable (Y)",
       y = "Predictor Value") +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10),
    legend.position = "none"
  )

# Commenting on observations based on boxplots
cat("\nComments on observations from the boxplots:\n")

# Loop through each weakest variable to make observations
for (var in weakest_vars) {
  # Check if there is a clear separation in the median (this is just a simple example)
  variable_values <- prostate_long[prostate_long$variable == var, ]
  median_cancer <- median(variable_values$value[variable_values$Y == 1], na.rm = TRUE)
  median_non_cancer <- median(variable_values$value[variable_values$Y == 0], na.rm = TRUE)

  if (abs(median_cancer - median_non_cancer) > 0.5) {  # Adjust threshold as needed
    cat(paste("For variable", var, ": There is a noticeable difference in the median values between cancer and non-cancer groups.\n"))
  } else {
    cat(paste("For variable", var, ": The median values between cancer and non-cancer groups are very similar, suggesting limited discriminative power.\n"))
  }

  # Check for differences in spread
  spread_cancer <- IQR(variable_values$value[variable_values$Y == 1], na.rm = TRUE)
  spread_non_cancer <- IQR(variable_values$value[variable_values$Y == 0], na.rm = TRUE)

  if (spread_cancer > spread_non_cancer) {
    cat(paste("For variable", var, ": The cancer group shows greater variability in the values compared to the non-cancer group.\n"))
  } else {
    cat(paste("For variable", var, ": The non-cancer group shows greater variability in the values compared to the cancer group.\n"))
  }
}
```

```{r}
#Question 9  Ensure required libraries are loaded
library(corrplot)    # For generating correlation plots
library(dplyr)       # For data manipulation
library(stringdist)  # For string matching

# Validate the top 9 predictors (Replace with actual column names from the dataset)
top_9_predictors <- c("X206212_at", "X207075_at", "X215872_at", "X12345_at", "X54321_at", 
                      "X67890_at", "X13579_at", "X24680_at", "X98765_at")

# Match predictors with actual column names in the dataset
matched_predictors <- sapply(top_9_predictors, function(x) {
  colnames(prostate)[which.min(stringdist(x, colnames(prostate), method = "osa"))]
})

# Filter out valid predictors
valid_predictors <- matched_predictors[matched_predictors %in% colnames(prostate)]

if (length(valid_predictors) > 0) {
  # Extract data for the valid predictors
  top_9_data <- prostate[, valid_predictors]
  
  # Ensure all columns are numeric
  top_9_data <- top_9_data %>% mutate_all(as.numeric)
  
  # Compute the correlation matrix (handle missing values using 'pairwise.complete.obs')
  cor_matrix <- cor(top_9_data, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
  
  # Generate a circular correlation plot
  corrplot(cor_matrix, method = "circle", 
           type = "upper",            # Display upper triangle
           tl.col = "black",          # Label color
           tl.srt = 45,               # Rotate labels for readability
           addCoef.col = "black",     # Add correlation coefficients
           number.cex = 0.7,          # Size of coefficient numbers
           main = "Circular Correlation Plot: Top 9 Predictors")  # Title
} else {
  print("No valid predictors found for correlation plot.")
}
# Add comments on what the correlation plot reveals
cat("\nCorrelation Plot Observations:\n")
cat("----------------------------------------------------\n")

# Comment on the general structure of the correlation plot
cat("1. The correlation plot displays the relationships between the top 9 predictor variables.\n")
cat("   - The size of the circles reflects the strength of the correlation between pairs of predictors.\n")
cat("   - Larger circles indicate stronger correlations, while smaller circles suggest weaker correlations.\n")

# Comment on the color scale
cat("2. The colors in the plot represent the direction of the correlation:\n")
cat("   - Red circles indicate a **positive correlation**, where both variables increase or decrease together.\n")
cat("   - Blue circles indicate a **negative correlation**, where one variable increases while the other decreases.\n")
cat("   - White circles represent **no correlation**, meaning there is no apparent relationship between the two variables.\n")

# Comment on interpreting high correlations
cat("3. High correlations (circles of large size and intense red or blue color) suggest that these predictors are related.\n")
cat("   - For example, if two predictors have a large red circle, they are both increasing or decreasing together.\n")
cat("   - If the correlation is negative (large blue circle), one predictor increases while the other decreases.\n")

# Comment on what to do with high correlations
cat("4. Strong correlations (above 0.8 or below -0.8) could indicate potential **multicollinearity**.\n")
cat("   - This means that some predictors are carrying redundant information, and including all of them in a model might lead to instability in the model coefficients.\n")
cat("   - Consider removing one of the highly correlated predictors to reduce redundancy.\n")

# Comment on low correlations
cat("5. Smaller circles suggest weaker correlations, which could imply that the predictors are independent of each other.\n")
cat("   - Such predictors may not provide as much shared information, which could be useful for building models.\n")

# Comment on the lack of diagonal correlations
cat("6. The diagonal is blank or excluded, as it represents self-correlation (where a variable is correlated with itself, which is always 1). This is redundant and not displayed.\n")

# General observations
cat("7. Overall, this correlation plot helps us identify relationships between predictors and assists in detecting multicollinearity issues.\n")
cat("   - If several predictors are highly correlated, removing one might simplify the model and improve model interpretability.\n")
cat("   - Conversely, weakly correlated predictors might carry independent and useful information for the model.\n")

cat("\n----------------------------------------------------\n")
```

```{r}
# Load the dataset
prostate <- read.csv("prostate-cancer-1.csv", header = TRUE, row.names = 1, check.names = FALSE)

# Compute the correlation matrix (exclude the response variable Y)
correlation_matrix <- cor(prostate[, -1])  # Exclude the response variable Y

# Perform eigendecomposition
eigen_decomp <- eigen(correlation_matrix)

# Extract eigenvalues
eigenvalues <- eigen_decomp$values

# Calculate the ratio λ_max / λ_min
lambda_max <- max(eigenvalues)
lambda_min <- min(eigenvalues)
lambda_ratio <- lambda_max / lambda_min

# Print the results
cat("Eigenvalues of the correlation matrix:", eigenvalues, "\n")
cat("Maximum Eigenvalue (λ_max):", lambda_max, "\n")
cat("Minimum Eigenvalue (λ_min):", lambda_min, "\n")
cat("Ratio (λ_max / λ_min):", lambda_ratio, "\n")

# Comment on the ratio
cat("\nInterpretation of the Ratio λ_max / λ_min:\n")
cat("----------------------------------------\n")
cat("1. The ratio of λ_max / λ_min indicates the condition number of the correlation matrix.\n")
cat("   - A high ratio suggests that the matrix is poorly conditioned, meaning that the data has high variance in some dimensions and low variance in others.\n")
cat("   - This could indicate issues such as multicollinearity in the dataset, where some predictors carry redundant information.\n")
cat("2. A ratio close to 1 indicates that the correlation matrix is well-conditioned, meaning that all predictors contribute roughly equally to the variability.\n")
cat("3. A very high ratio (much greater than 1) could suggest that the dataset may have a problematic structure, possibly due to highly correlated predictors.\n")
cat("   - This could lead to instability in statistical models, especially in regression analysis.\n")
cat("4. A small λ_min suggests that there is one or more directions (principal components) in the data with low variance, which could indicate near-linear dependence among predictors.\n")
cat("   - In such cases, dimensionality reduction techniques such as PCA might be useful.\n")
cat("\n----------------------------------------\n")
```

```{r}
# Question 11 Load necessary libraries
# Load necessary libraries
library(class)   # For k-NN classifier
library(rpart)   # For decision tree classifierauthor{}
library(ROCR)    # For ROC curve
library(ggplot2) # For plotting

# Read dataset
prostate <- read.csv('prostate-cancer-1.csv')
prostate$Y <- as.factor(prostate$Y)  # Ensure response is a factor

# Define the predictor variables (excluding the response variable 'Y')
predictors <- setdiff(names(prostate), 'Y')

# Create training and testing datasets (using the whole data for training and testing)
X <- prostate[, predictors]
y <- prostate$Y

# Initialize a list to store ROC curve data for each model
roc_data_list <- list()

# 1. 1NN Model
knn_1 <- knn(X, X, y, k = 1)
pred_knn_1 <- as.numeric(knn_1) - 1  # Convert to 0 and 1 (0 = negative, 1 = positive)
pred_knn_1_roc <- prediction(pred_knn_1, as.numeric(y) - 1)
roc_knn_1 <- performance(pred_knn_1_roc, "tpr", "fpr")
roc_data_list$knn_1 <- list(fpr = roc_knn_1@x.values[[1]], tpr = roc_knn_1@y.values[[1]])

# 2. 7NN Model
knn_7 <- knn(X, X, y, k = 7)
pred_knn_7 <- as.numeric(knn_7) - 1
pred_knn_7_roc <- prediction(pred_knn_7, as.numeric(y) - 1)
roc_knn_7 <- performance(pred_knn_7_roc, "tpr", "fpr")
roc_data_list$knn_7 <- list(fpr = roc_knn_7@x.values[[1]], tpr = roc_knn_7@y.values[[1]])

# 3. 9NN Model
knn_9 <- knn(X, X, y, k = 9)
pred_knn_9 <- as.numeric(knn_9) - 1
pred_knn_9_roc <- prediction(pred_knn_9, as.numeric(y) - 1)
roc_knn_9 <- performance(pred_knn_9_roc, "tpr", "fpr")
roc_data_list$knn_9 <- list(fpr = roc_knn_9@x.values[[1]], tpr = roc_knn_9@y.values[[1]])

# 4. Decision Tree Model (cp = 0)
tree_cp0 <- rpart(Y ~ ., data = prostate, method = "class", control = rpart.control(cp = 0))
pred_tree_cp0 <- predict(tree_cp0, type = "prob")[, 2]  # Get the probability for the positive class
pred_tree_cp0_roc <- prediction(pred_tree_cp0, as.numeric(y) - 1)
roc_tree_cp0 <- performance(pred_tree_cp0_roc, "tpr", "fpr")
roc_data_list$tree_cp0 <- list(fpr = roc_tree_cp0@x.values[[1]], tpr = roc_tree_cp0@y.values[[1]])

# 5. Decision Tree Model (cp = 0.05)
tree_cp005 <- rpart(Y ~ ., data = prostate, method = "class", control = rpart.control(cp = 0.05))
pred_tree_cp005 <- predict(tree_cp005, type = "prob")[, 2]
pred_tree_cp005_roc <- prediction(pred_tree_cp005, as.numeric(y) - 1)
roc_tree_cp005 <- performance(pred_tree_cp005_roc, "tpr", "fpr")
roc_data_list$tree_cp005 <- list(fpr = roc_tree_cp005@x.values[[1]], tpr = roc_tree_cp005@y.values[[1]])

# 6. Decision Tree Model (cp = 0.1)
tree_cp01 <- rpart(Y ~ ., data = prostate, method = "class", control = rpart.control(cp = 0.1))
pred_tree_cp01 <- predict(tree_cp01, type = "prob")[, 2]
pred_tree_cp01_roc <- prediction(pred_tree_cp01, as.numeric(y) - 1)
roc_tree_cp01 <- performance(pred_tree_cp01_roc, "tpr", "fpr")
roc_data_list$tree_cp01 <- list(fpr = roc_tree_cp01@x.values[[1]], tpr = roc_tree_cp01@y.values[[1]])

# Ensure all ROC data exists
if(length(roc_data_list) != 6) {
  cat("Error: Some models are missing from the ROC data list.")
}

# Plot all ROC curves on the same grid with different line types
plot(roc_data_list$knn_1$fpr, roc_data_list$knn_1$tpr, type = "l", col = "blue", lty = 1,
     main = "Comparative ROC Curves for 1NN, 7NN, 9NN, and Decision Trees", 
     xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "False Positive Rate", ylab = "True Positive Rate")
lines(roc_data_list$knn_7$fpr, roc_data_list$knn_7$tpr, col = "green", lty = 2)
lines(roc_data_list$knn_9$fpr, roc_data_list$knn_9$tpr, col = "red", lty = 3)
lines(roc_data_list$tree_cp0$fpr, roc_data_list$tree_cp0$tpr, col = "purple", lty = 4)
lines(roc_data_list$tree_cp005$fpr, roc_data_list$tree_cp005$tpr, col = "orange", lty = 5)
lines(roc_data_list$tree_cp01$fpr, roc_data_list$tree_cp01$tpr, col = "brown", lty = 6)

# Add legend to differentiate each model
legend("bottomright", legend = c("1NN", "7NN", "9NN", "Tree (cp=0)", "Tree (cp=0.05)", "Tree (cp=0.1)"),
       col = c("blue", "green", "red", "purple", "orange", "brown"), 
       lty = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6), cex = 0.8)

```

```{r}
# Load necessary libraries
library(rpart)          # For decision tree classification
library(rpart.plot)     # For plotting the decision tree

# Read dataset
prostate <- read.csv('prostate-cancer-1.csv')
prostate$Y <- as.factor(prostate$Y)  # Ensure response is a factor

# Build classification trees with different cp values
tree_cp0 <- rpart(Y ~ ., data = prostate, method = "class", control = rpart.control(cp = 0))
tree_cp005 <- rpart(Y ~ ., data = prostate, method = "class", control = rpart.control(cp = 0.05))

prp(tree_cp0, type = 4, extra = 1, fallen.leaves = TRUE, 
    main = "Classification Tree (cp = 0)", 
    box.col = "lightblue", branch.col = "darkgreen", 
    shadow.col = "gray", nn = TRUE)

# Tree with cp = 0.05
prp(tree_cp005, type = 4, extra = 1, fallen.leaves = TRUE, 
    main = "Classification Tree (cp = 0.05)", 
    box.col = "lightgreen", branch.col = "darkblue", 
    shadow.col = "gray", nn = TRUE)

# Tree with cp = 0.1
prp(tree_cp01, type = 4, extra = 1, fallen.leaves = TRUE, 
    main = "Classification Tree (cp = 0.1)", 
    box.col = "lightyellow", branch.col = "darkred", 
    shadow.col = "gray", nn = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#Question 14: Load necessary libraries
library(class)           # For k-NN
library(rpart)           # For decision trees
library(ROCR)            # For performance metrics
library(caret)           # For resampling
library(lattice)
library(ggplot2)         # For plotting
library(dplyr)           # For data manipulation

# Set seed for reproducibility
set.seed(19671210)

# Load the prostate dataset
prostate <- read.csv('prostate-cancer-1.csv')
prostate$Y <- as.factor(prostate$Y)  # Ensure the response variable is a factor

# Define models
models <- list(
  "1NN" = function(train_data, train_labels, test_data) knn(train_data, test_data, train_labels, k = 1),
  "7NN" = function(train_data, train_labels, test_data) knn(train_data, test_data, train_labels, k = 7),
  "9NN" = function(train_data, train_labels, test_data) knn(train_data, test_data, train_labels, k = 9),
  "Tree_cp0" = function(train_data, train_labels, test_data) {
    model <- rpart(Y ~ ., data = train_data, method = "class", control = rpart.control(cp = 0))
    predict(model, test_data, type = "class")
  },
  "Tree_cp005" = function(train_data, train_labels, test_data) {
    model <- rpart(Y ~ ., data = train_data, method = "class", control = rpart.control(cp = 0.05))
    predict(model, test_data, type = "class")
  },
  "Tree_cp01" = function(train_data, train_labels, test_data) {
    model <- rpart(Y ~ ., data = train_data, method = "class", control = rpart.control(cp = 0.1))
    predict(model, test_data, type = "class")
  }
)

# Function to compute test error (misclassification rate)
compute_test_error <- function(predictions, true_labels) {
  mean(predictions != true_labels)
}

# Perform 100 replications of random holdout splits
S <- 100
test_errors <- data.frame(matrix(ncol = length(models), nrow = S))
colnames(test_errors) <- names(models)

for (i in 1:S) {
  # Perform a 7/10 training, 3/10 testing split
  train_index <- createDataPartition(prostate$Y, p = 0.7, list = FALSE)
  train_data <- prostate[train_index, ]
  test_data <- prostate[-train_index, ]
  
  # Get the training labels and test labels
  train_labels <- train_data$Y
  test_labels <- test_data$Y
  
  # For each model, fit and compute the test error
  for (model_name in names(models)) {
    model_func <- models[[model_name]]
    predictions <- model_func(train_data, train_labels, test_data)
    test_errors[i, model_name] <- compute_test_error(predictions, test_labels)
  }
}

# Plot comparative boxplots of test errors
test_errors_long <- reshape2::melt(test_errors)
colnames(test_errors_long) <- c("Model", "TestError")
ggplot(test_errors_long, aes(x = Model, y = TestError, fill = Model)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "Comparative Boxplots of Test Errors (100 Replications)",
       x = "Learning Machine", y = "Test Error") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

# Perform ANOVA on the test errors
anova_result <- aov(TestError ~ Model, data = test_errors_long)
summary(anova_result)

```

```{r}
#Question 2: Load necessary libraries
# Load necessary libraries
library(dslabs)   # To load the MNIST data
library(class)    # For k-NN classifier
library(caret)    # For resampling and evaluation metrics
library(ggplot2)  # For plotting results
library(dplyr)    # For data manipulation

# Read MNIST data
mnist <- read_mnist()   # Load the MNIST dataset

# Training and Test Data
xtrain <- mnist$train$images
ytrain <- mnist$train$labels
ytrain <- as.factor(ytrain)  # Convert labels to factor for classification

xtest <- mnist$test$images
ytest <- mnist$test$labels
ytest <- as.factor(ytest)  # Convert labels to factor for classification

# Number of training and testing examples
ntr <- nrow(xtrain)
p <- ncol(xtrain)  # Number of features (pixels)

# Choose n (training size) and m (test size) for a smaller sample
n <- 1000   # Size of training data
m <- 1000   # Size of test data

# Set random seed for reproducibility
set.seed(42)

# Sample n random training samples and m random test samples
train_indices <- sample(1:ntr, n)
xtrain_sample <- xtrain[train_indices, ]  # Sampled training images
ytrain_sample <- ytrain[train_indices]    # Sampled training labels

test_indices <- sample(1:length(ytest), m)
xtest_sample <- xtest[test_indices, ]  # Sampled test images
ytest_sample <- ytest[test_indices]    # Sampled test labels

# Display the size of the sampled training and test sets
cat("Training set size:", nrow(xtrain_sample), "\n")
cat("Test set size:", nrow(xtest_sample), "\n")

# Function to compute the accuracy of the model
compute_accuracy <- function(predictions, true_labels) {
  sum(predictions == true_labels) / length(true_labels)
}

# List of different k-values for k-NN classifier
k_values <- c(1, 5, 7, 9, 13)

# Train k-NN models and evaluate their accuracy
results <- data.frame(Model = character(), Accuracy = numeric())

for (k in k_values) {
  # Train k-NN model with current k
  predictions <- knn(xtrain_sample, xtest_sample, ytrain_sample, k = k)
  
  # Compute accuracy
  accuracy <- compute_accuracy(predictions, ytest_sample)
  
  # Store the results
  results <- rbind(results, data.frame(Model = paste(k, "NN"), Accuracy = accuracy))
}

# Print results
print(results)

# Plot the accuracy results
ggplot(results, aes(x = Model, y = Accuracy, fill = Model)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", color = "black", width = 0.6) +
  labs(title = "Accuracy of k-NN Classifier for Different k-values",
       x = "Model (k-NN)",
       y = "Accuracy") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

```{r}
suppressWarnings({
  library(dslabs)
  library(class)

# Suppress warnings to keep the output clean
suppressWarnings({
  library(dslabs)
  library(class)
  library(caret)
  library(ggplot2)
  library(lattice)
})

# Load the MNIST data
mnist <- read_mnist() # Read in the MNIST data
xtrain <- mnist$train$images
ytrain <- mnist$train$labels
ytrain <- as.factor(ytrain)
xtest <- mnist$test$images
ytest <- mnist$test$labels
ytest <- as.factor(ytest)

# Set random seed for reproducibility
set.seed(123)

# Define the k-NN models with different values of k
knn_models <- list(
  "1NN" = function(train_data, train_labels, test_data) knn(train_data, test_data, train_labels, k = 1),
  "5NN" = function(train_data, train_labels, test_data) knn(train_data, test_data, train_labels, k = 5),
  "7NN" = function(train_data, train_labels, test_data) knn(train_data, test_data, train_labels, k = 7),
  "9NN" = function(train_data, train_labels, test_data) knn(train_data, test_data, train_labels, k = 9),
  "13NN" = function(train_data, train_labels, test_data) knn(train_data, test_data, train_labels, k = 13)
)

# Number of random splits
S <- 50
test_errors <- matrix(NA, nrow = S, ncol = length(knn_models))
colnames(test_errors) <- names(knn_models)

# Perform 50 random splits, compute test errors, and store results
for (i in 1:S) {
  # Randomly split the data into 70% training and 30% test
  train_indices <- sample(1:nrow(xtrain), 0.7 * nrow(xtrain))
  xtrain_split <- xtrain[train_indices, ]
  ytrain_split <- ytrain[train_indices]
  xtest_split <- xtrain[-train_indices, ]
  ytest_split <- ytrain[-train_indices]
  
  # Compute test errors for each model
  for (model_name in names(knn_models)) {
    model_func <- knn_models[[model_name]]
    predictions <- model_func(xtrain_split, ytrain_split, xtest_split)
    test_errors[i, model_name] <- mean(predictions != ytest_split)
  }
}

# Convert the matrix to a data frame for easier handling
test_errors_df <- as.data.frame(test_errors)

# Display the first few rows of test errors
head(test_errors_df)

# Part 2: Identify the model with the smallest median test error
median_errors <- apply(test_errors_df, 2, median)
best_model_name <- names(median_errors)[which.min(median_errors)]
cat("The best model is:", best_model_name, "with the smallest median test error.\n")

# Perform a test prediction for the best model on the last split
best_model_func <- knn_models[[best_model_name]]
predictions_best_model <- best_model_func(xtrain_split, ytrain_split, xtest_split)

# Generate confusion matrix for the best model
confusion_matrix <- table(Predicted = predictions_best_model, Actual = ytest_split)
cat("Confusion Matrix for the best model:\n")
print(confusion_matrix)

# Part 3: Comment on digits with the most confusion
# In the confusion matrix, the most confused digits are those with a higher count in the off-diagonal cells.
# We can analyze the matrix and look at the digits that often get confused.

# Part 4: Perform an ANOVA to analyze test errors across different models
test_errors_df_long <- reshape(test_errors_df, 
                               varying = names(test_errors_df),
                               v.names = "Error", 
                               times = names(test_errors_df),
                               timevar = "Model", 
                               times = names(test_errors_df),
                               direction = "long")

anova_result <- aov(Error ~ Model, data = test_errors_df_long)
cat("ANOVA results:\n")
print(summary(anova_result))

# Comment on ANOVA: Based on the ANOVA results, we can comment on whether the differences between models
# are statistically significant and which models perform better on average.
```
